tier_reason: hiae-aead/benchmarks runs ROCCA-S (rocca-s/performance_test.c + rocca-s/rocca-s.c) against OpenSSL EVP AES-128-GCM/CTR (aes128-gcm-openssl/benchmark.c + encrypt.c) through a top-level Makefile, and the README states the compilers (Apple clang 21.0.0, clang 21.1.8), flags (-O3 -march=native, -mcpu=native on ARM), CPUs (Apple M5 Max, Ryzen 7 7700 at 3.8 GHz fixed) and OpenSSL versions. That is public code plus full methodology, so it is tier A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: At 64 KB on Apple M5 Max, ROCCA-S AEAD runs at 208.1 Gbps encryption and 140.4 Gbps decryption, against OpenSSL AES-128-GCM's 70.8 and 70.2 Gbps (~2.9x encryption, ~2.0x decryption, derived from page data). Its keystream path runs at 228.8 Gbps against OpenSSL AES-128-CTR's 159.6 (~1.4x, derived from page data). On Zen 4 (Ryzen 7 7700 locked at 3.8 GHz), ROCCA-S does 174.6 Gbps encryption and 92.3 Gbps decryption, against AES-128-GCM's 92.7 and 92.9 Gbps. That is ~1.9x on encryption, but decryption is at parity, about 0.99x (derived from page data; the Zen 4 GCM figures appear only in the README's bar chart).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: M5: Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -mcpu=native (the Makefile uses -mcpu=native on arm64), with OpenSSL 3.6.4. Zen 4: clang 21.1.8, -O3 -march=native, with OpenSSL 3.5.5. All builds also use -std=c99.
corrections.workload: AEAD encryption and decryption throughput at 64 KB messages, with 48-byte associated data plus the tag, sweeping sizes from 16 B to 64 KB. A separate keystream-only mode is compared against OpenSSL AES-128-CTR. Buffers are 4096-byte aligned. Measured on Apple M5 Max and AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2 stars. KDDI's official reference implementation of Rocca-S (ESORICS 2023: 'An Ultra-High Throughput AES-based Authenticated Encryption Scheme for 6G'). The spec is IETF individual draft draft-nakano-rocca-s-06 (2026-01-28). It was presented at CFRG IETF-115, was never adopted, and expired on 2026-08-01.
corrections.caveats: The comparison numbers come from a separate repo, hiae-aead/benchmarks. It lives under the HiAE org, almost all commits are by jedisct1, and it has no top-level license. Its rocca-s/rocca-s.c is a reformatted copy of KDDI's MIT reference with an added ARM-crypto (vaeseq/vaesmcq) backend, so the M5 figures measure that port, not yt-nakano's code as-is; yt-nakano's code supports only x86 AES-NI plus a portable table fallback. The yt-nakano README itself gives only a standalone '>200 Gbps on i9-12900K' figure with no baseline. The comparison is 256-bit-key Rocca-S against AES-128-GCM, not the like-for-like AES-256-GCM. Decryption is much slower than encryption (1.48x slower on M5, 1.89x on Zen 4), and on Zen 4 decryption only matches OpenSSL's VAES GCM. On security, Rocca-S is not key-committing. Practical FROB committing attacks with a test vector are in Takeuchi-Todo-Iwata, ePrint 2024/901, which extends their ToSC 2024(2) attack on revised Rocca and improves Derbez et al., ToSC 2024(1), which needed 2^64. The same note found an equivalent-key issue in the short-key expansion, fixed in draft-06; the reference code takes 256-bit keys only. The ToSC 2024(2) key-recovery and universal-forgery results target Rocca-v2/v3/v4, not Rocca-S; the paper notes that Rocca-S shares v4's unkeyed finalization and leaves Rocca-S open. I found no published key-recovery or nonce-respecting forgery against Rocca-S.

notes: Numbers match the README tables exactly (M5 table; Zen 4 ROCCA-S row plus the Zen 4 chart for GCM), and tier A holds. The main correction is that on Zen 4 ROCCA-S decryption (92.3 Gbps) only ties OpenSSL AES-128-GCM (92.9 Gbps), so the win there is encryption-only. The record's language 'C++' is wrong: the reference code is C, and only its gtest tests are C++. That field cannot be corrected in this schema, so the orchestrator should fix it. License MIT, 2 stars, last commit 2025-03-19 and 'stale' all check out.
